newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin meets PM as new budget battle looms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin meets PM as new budget battle looms.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, back in the Kremlin after May Day holidays, met senior officials on Monday to discuss national security and economic reforms as his government prepared for battle over unpopular spending cuts.

In talks with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin focused on chronic wage arrears -- Russia's number one social problem affecting millions of workers -- and on seeking parliamentary backing for the new austerity plans.

Yeltsin also met Ivan Rybkin, secretary of the policy-making Security Council, to discuss Moscow's delicate relations with the breakaway region of Chechnya and the development of a new doctrine of national security.
Later on Monday, Yeltsin was due to attend a welcome ceremony in the Kremlin for King Juan Carlos of Spain at the start of a three-day state visit.
The flurry of engagements followed a break for the 66-year-old president, first at the Black Sea resort of Sochi and then at a country residence outside Moscow.
Yeltsin is keen to keep up the political momentum from his promotion of pro-market liberals to top economic positions in the government in March.

Chernomyrdin is expected go to the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, on May 21 to try to persuade lawmakers to swallow the spending cuts, aimed at bridging a yawning gap between revenues and spending.
Mikhail Zadornov, head of the Duma's budget committee, said he had received the spending bill, which a government official said would cut about one fifth of the 1997 budget.

Zadornov told Reuters that deputies, who only approved the original budget after months of angry debate, might retaliate with calls to print money to keep spending on track. Yeltsin has vowed not to take such a course, which would reignite inflation.

Russia's budget gap has been an important concern for the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which has suspended disbursing a $10 billion three-year loan because of low tax revenues. Officials say they expect payment to resume this month.
Chernomyrdin said he hoped the Duma, dominated by Yeltsin's communist foes, would show "a spirit of responsibility and cooperation" over the budget cuts.

Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin also agreed that the prime minister should go to Ukraine on May 28-29 to help patch up Russia's frayed relations with its Slav neighbour before a much-postponed visit to Kiev by Yeltsin himself, probably in June.

The presidential press service said Russia's Security Council would meet on May 7 to discuss a new national security doctrine, widely seen as a prerequisite for a planned overhaul of the cash-strapped armed forces.

Rybkin told Interfax news agency that Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov would soon meet Yeltsin in Moscow after officials completed documents charting a new relationship between Russia and the secessionist North Caucasus region. The two sides fought a 21-month war until last August.
Russia has beefed up security in recent days after two bomb explosions in the southern towns of Armavir and Pyatigorsk, both near Chechnya, killed four people.
Radical Chechen commander Salman Raduyev has claimed responsibility for the attacks and on Monday the Chechen authorities issued an arrest warrant for him.
Rybkin said Yeltsin had agreed to the setting up of a joint Russian-Chechen commission to investigate the blasts, which have threatened to derail the difficult peace talks.
Sounding an optimistic note about the negotiations, Rybkin told Interfax: "There will be no lack of good will from the federal (Russian) side."
Raduyev, an isolated figure who is not part of Chechnya's post-war separatist leadership, has often vowed to attack Russian targets over Moscow's refusal to recognise his country's independence.
